purpose: Every candidate tag for screening restaurants, with its real properties. Four families. No composite score is computed from these -- they are tags, filterable individually. The suitability scale remains undefined by design.

families.curatorial: Third-party recognition. Bootstraps a list, indicates competence, predicts nothing about accommodation.
families.structural: Facts about how the menu and service are ORGANIZED. Machine-readable, globally uniform, free to store. The workhorse family.
families.camouflage: Whether ordering the way you need to order looks like how everyone else orders. The 'no big deal' axis.
families.accommodation_evidence: What the kitchen will actually do. Historically contact-only; two members of this family are machine-readable, which is the important finding.

signals.label: Award tier (verbatim)
signals.what_it_tells_you: that a third party rated the kitchen highly
signals.why_it_works: bounded, citable, externally defined -- good for a seed list
signals.caveat: No relationship to accommodation willingness. Michelin skews to expensive protein-centred tasting menus, which are among the hardest cases.

signals.label: Menu published online at all
signals.what_it_tells_you: whether you can plan before arriving
signals.why_it_works: the precondition for everything else; also the single most common failure
signals.caveat: A stale undated 'sample menu' PDF counts as published and is often wrong.

signals.label: Dishes have ingredient descriptions
signals.what_it_tells_you: whether the census can extract anything
signals.why_it_works: name-only menus ('Market Fish 34') are unanalysable at any scale

signals.label: A la carte (not tasting-only)
signals.what_it_tells_you: whether you can choose what arrives
signals.why_it_works: a fixed progression removes the diner's only real lever
signals.caveat: Tasting-only is not fatal if the kitchen swaps courses -- but that is accommodation data, not structure.

signals.label: Number of standalone sides / vegetable plates
signals.what_it_tells_you: how much of a meal you can build without asking for anything
signals.why_it_works: sides are the composable unit; a long sides list is a menu you can eat from silently
signals.caveat: Counts dishes, not portions. Four sides may still not be dinner.

signals.label: Distinct starch families named
signals.what_it_tells_you: whether there is more than one calorie base, so one being off-menu is not fatal
signals.why_it_works: single-anchor menus are a single point of failure

signals.label: Allergen or dietary matrix published
signals.global_coverage: strong in EU/UK, weak in US
signals.what_it_tells_you: that the kitchen tracks ingredients per dish as a routine
signals.why_it_works: EU allergen regulation forced this infrastructure into existence; where it exists the kitchen already has per-dish ingredient discipline
signals.caveat: Allergen data is about the 14 declarable allergens, NOT protein quantity. Useful as evidence of ingredient tracking, never as a phe source.

signals.label: Online ordering exists
signals.what_it_tells_you: that a structured, machine-readable menu exists behind it
signals.why_it_works: ordering platforms expose menus as JSON -- far better than scraping a design-led site

signals.label: Online-order modifier groups (remove cheese, sub side)
signals.what_it_tells_you: that the kitchen ALREADY has a workflow for altering this dish -- and you can invoke it without speaking to anyone
signals.why_it_works: This is the finding worth acting on. Accommodation was assumed to be contact-only, but a modifier group is a kitchen capability the restaurant has published in machine-readable form. If Toast lets a stranger uncheck cheese at 11pm, the line cook has a process for a plate without cheese.
signals.caveat: Proves the modifier exists, not that staff apply it correctly, and covers only dishes sold online. It is evidence, not verification -- it can raise a restaurant to 'evidenced', never to 'verified'.

signals.label: Reservation special-request free-text field
signals.what_it_tells_you: that a written request reaches the kitchen before you arrive
signals.why_it_works: present on every major booking platform, needs no partnership or API key, and is the integration point that actually exists today
signals.caveat: Delivery to the kitchen is not guaranteed and nothing is confirmed back.

signals.label: Dedicated dietary-accommodation page or statement
signals.what_it_tells_you: that the restaurant has thought about dietary requests before you called

signals.label: Structured community visit report
signals.what_it_tells_you: what the kitchen actually did, for a real diner, on a real night
signals.why_it_works: The scaling engine. This is the TripAdvisor analogue -- but the unit is a structured report, not a star rating. A star tells you nothing; 'asked for the polenta without cheese, they did it, gave me the gram weight' is reusable data. It is also the only way to populate the accommodation axis faster than the team can make phone calls.
signals.caveat: Self-selected sample, single-night observation, and staff turnover ages it. Expires like any verification.

signals.label: Direct verification by contact
signals.what_it_tells_you: what the kitchen commits to, on the record
signals.why_it_works: the only tag that can carry a badge
signals.caveat: Expensive per restaurant. Expires after 180 days.

signals.label: Composing your own meal is the house format
signals.what_it_tells_you: that ordering four vegetable plates is what the menu is FOR
signals.why_it_works: Tapas, mezze, dim sum, izakaya, meze, banchan, small-plates: everyone at the table orders this way, so a low-protein order is invisible. This is the single strongest camouflage signal and it is fully machine-readable from menu structure.

signals.label: Counter, kiosk or app ordering
signals.what_it_tells_you: that no server conversation is required at all
signals.why_it_works: the lowest-friction service model there is: you tap what you want and nobody asks why
signals.caveat: Counter service often means fewer modifications are possible, so camouflage and flexibility can trade off.

signals.label: Build-your-own item on the menu
signals.what_it_tells_you: that per-component choice is a published, priced option
signals.why_it_works: customisation is the product, so specifying components is ordinary

signals.label: Vegetables appear as centre-of-plate dishes
signals.what_it_tells_you: that ordering a vegetable dish as your main is unremarkable
signals.why_it_works: removes the 'is that all you're having?' moment, which is most of the social cost
signals.caveat: Vegetable-forward does NOT mean low protein. Legume, cheese and nut-heavy vegetarian dishes are frequently the highest-phe items on a menu.

signals.label: Kids menu present
signals.what_it_tells_you: that plain preparations exist and small portions are already priced
signals.why_it_works: a kids menu is institutionalised plain food, and ordering from it draws no attention when a child is at the table
signals.caveat: Kids menus are usually breaded, fried and cheese-heavy. Weak signal, cheap to collect.

explicitly_rejected.why: Two independent reasons. Legally, Google's Places policies forbid pre-fetching, caching or storing Places content beyond narrow exceptions -- only place_id may be stored indefinitely and coordinates for up to 30 days -- so a stored rating is a terms violation and every render is a billable live call. Substantively, a crowd rating measures whether a restaurant is good, which is not the question. A 4.8-star steakhouse can be a 0 for us and a 3.9-star tapas bar can be a 4.
explicitly_rejected.what_to_keep_instead: place_id only, as a stable global join key. It is storable indefinitely, it is not editorial, and it makes every other data source line up across cities.

explicitly_rejected.signal: 'Gluten-free available' as a proxy for low protein
explicitly_rejected.why: Actively dangerous and the most common wrong inference in this whole domain. Gluten-free baking substitutes almond, chickpea and soy flour -- frequently HIGHER phe than wheat. Kept only as evidence of ingredient-tracking infrastructure, never as a dietary signal.

explicitly_rejected.signal: 'Vegan' or 'vegetarian' as a proxy for low protein
explicitly_rejected.why: Same error. Legumes, tofu, seitan, nuts and cheese are among the highest-phe foods on any menu. A vegan restaurant can be the worst option in a city.
Expensive restaurants are protein-cut-focused; cheap ones are starch-heavy. If anything the correlation runs against intuition, and it is not strong enough in either direction to be worth a tag.

design_note: No composite is computed. These are independent filters, each with its own provenance and its own failure mode. Collapsing them into one number would be the suitability scale, which is deferred.
